claim: Microsporidia are strict intracellular eukaryotic parasites that infect a broad range of animal hosts, including humans and economically important species of fish, honeybees, and silkworms.
source: Microsporidia are a highly successful group of strict intracellular eukaryotic parasites that infect a broad range of animal hosts, including humans and economically important species of fish, honeybees, and silkworms (Stentiford et al., 2016; Vávra and Lukeš, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Stentiford et al., 2016; Vávra and Lukeš, 2013).

claim: Microsporidia can only complete their life cycle inside infected eukaryotic cells.
source: Microsporidia can only complete their life cycle inside infected eukaryotic cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about Microsporidia biology.

claim: In the external environment Microsporidia exist only as resistant thick-walled spores.
source: In the external environment they exist only as resistant thick-walled spores.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about Microsporidia biology.

claim: New Microsporidia infections are initiated by spore germination followed by transit of the parasite through a unique polar tube infection apparatus into a eukaryotic host cell.
source: New infections are then initiated by spore germination followed by transit of the parasite through a unique polar tube infection apparatus into a eukaryotic host cell (Vávra and Lukeš, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Vávra and Lukeš, 2013).

claim: Microsporidia have undergone dramatic genomic and cellular streamlining including the complete loss of biosynthetic pathways for de novo synthesis of purine and pyrimidine nucleotides.
source: As a result of this lifestyle, Microsporidia have undergone dramatic genomic and cellular streamlining including the complete loss of biosynthetic pathways for de novo synthesis of purine and pyrimidine nucleotides (Dean et al., 2016; Dean et al., 2018; Heinz et al., 2014; Heinz et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Dean et al., 2016; Dean et al., 2018; Heinz et al., 2014; Heinz et al., 2012).

claim: Microsporidia mitochondria (called mitosomes) have lost the organelle genome and the capacity to generate ATP.
source: At the organelle level, reduction is dramatically illustrated by their minimal mitochondria (called mitosomes) which have lost the organelle genome and the capacity to generate ATP (Freibert et al., 2017; Goldberg et al., 2008; Williams et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Freibert et al., 2017; Goldberg et al., 2008; Williams et al., 2002).

claim: Glycolysis is conserved in some, but not all Microsporidia.
source: While glycolysis is conserved in some, but not all (Wiredu Boakye et al., 2017) Microsporidia, it appears to be mainly active in spores and is not used during intracellular growth and replication (Dolgikh et al., 2011; Heinz et al., 2012; Williams et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Wiredu Boakye et al., 2017).

claim: Microsporidia glycolysis appears to be mainly active in spores and is not used during intracellular growth and replication.
source: While glycolysis is conserved in some, but not all (Wiredu Boakye et al., 2017) Microsporidia, it appears to be mainly active in spores and is not used during intracellular growth and replication (Dolgikh et al., 2011; Heinz et al., 2012; Williams et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Dolgikh et al., 2011; Heinz et al., 2012; Williams et al., 2014).

claim: Microsporidia are entirely dependent upon the host cells they infect for the energy, cofactors and nucleic acid building blocks that they need to complete their life cycle.
source: The loss of indigenous pathways for making ATP and nucleotides means that Microsporidia are now entirely dependent upon the host cells they infect for the energy, cofactors and nucleic acid building blocks that they need to complete their life cycle (Dean et al., 2016; Nakjang et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Dean et al., 2016; Nakjang et al., 2013) and logical inference from the loss of biosynthetic pathways.

claim: Parasite transport proteins must play critical roles in servicing the energetic and metabolic demands imposed by Microsporidia growth and replication.
source: Hence parasite transport proteins must play critical roles in servicing the energetic and metabolic demands imposed by parasite growth and replication, but there is currently little functional data for Microsporidia transporters (Dean et al., 2016; Dean et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the dependence on host metabolites and the need for transport proteins to acquire them.

claim: There is currently little functional data for Microsporidia transporters.
source: Hence parasite transport proteins must play critical roles in servicing the energetic and metabolic demands imposed by parasite growth and replication, but there is currently little functional data for Microsporidia transporters (Dean et al., 2016; Dean et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Dean et al., 2016; Dean et al., 2014).

claim: Microsporidia have far fewer (~2000–3500) protein-encoding genes than free-living eukaryotes.
source: Microsporidia have far fewer (~2000–3500) protein-encoding genes than free-living eukaryotes, providing strong evidence that gene loss, particularly for metabolism, is a pervasive feature of their evolution (Cuomo et al., 2012; Nakjang et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Cuomo et al., 2012; Nakjang et al., 2013).

claim: Gene loss, particularly for metabolism, is a pervasive feature of Microsporidia evolution.
source: Microsporidia have far fewer (~2000–3500) protein-encoding genes than free-living eukaryotes, providing strong evidence that gene loss, particularly for metabolism, is a pervasive feature of their evolution (Cuomo et al., 2012; Nakjang et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Cuomo et al., 2012; Nakjang et al., 2013).

claim: Genes for candidate surface-located transporters that have been retained against the background of gene loss are likely to be important for supporting parasite growth and replication.
source: Genes for candidate surface-located transporters that have been retained against this background of gene loss, are likely to be important for supporting parasite growth and replication (Heinz et al., 2012; Nakjang et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the selective retention of genes and supported by citations (Heinz et al., 2012; Nakjang et al., 2013).

claim: Ten gene families encoding candidate surface transport proteins are conserved in all published Microsporidia genomes.
source: We previously identified 10 gene families encoding candidate surface transport proteins that are conserved in all published Microsporidia genomes (Heinz et al., 2012; Nakjang et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Heinz et al., 2012; Nakjang et al., 2013).

claim: Microsporidia NTT transporters are expressed on the cell surface of intracellular Microsporidia where they can import host purine nucleotides, including ATP, GTP and NAD+.
source: The conserved families include the experimentally characterised nucleotide transporters (NTT) that are expressed on the cell surface of intracellular Microsporidia where they can import host purine nucleotides, including ATP, GTP and NAD+ (Dean et al., 2016; Dean et al., 2014; Dean et al., 2018; Tsaousis et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Dean et al., 2016; Dean et al., 2014; Dean et al., 2018; Tsaousis et al., 2008).

claim: NTT transporters did not transport pyrimidine nucleotides in experiments.
source: Intriguingly, the NTT transporters did not transport pyrimidine nucleotides in these experiments (Dean et al., 2018; Heinz et al., 2014), even though genome analyses suggest that Microsporidia can no longer make these substrates for themselves (Dean et al., 2016; Dean et al., 2018; Heinz et al., 2014; Tsaousis et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Dean et al., 2018; Heinz et al., 2014).

claim: Genome analyses suggest that Microsporidia can no longer make pyrimidine nucleotides for themselves.
source: Intriguingly, the NTT transporters did not transport pyrimidine nucleotides in these experiments (Dean et al., 2018; Heinz et al., 2014), even though genome analyses suggest that Microsporidia can no longer make these substrates for themselves (Dean et al., 2016; Dean et al., 2018; Heinz et al., 2014; Tsaousis et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Dean et al., 2016; Dean et al., 2018; Heinz et al., 2014; Tsaousis et al., 2008).

claim: Additional transporters must exist to supply Microsporidia with the pyrimidines that they need to grow and replicate.
source: These data suggest that additional transporters must exist to supply Microsporidia with the pyrimidines that they need to grow and replicate.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the inability of NTT transporters to transport pyrimidines and the need for pyrimidines.

claim: A family of Microsporidia Major Facilitator Superfamily (MFS) transport proteins was discovered in Nematocida spp.
source: In the present study, we have characterised a family of Microsporidia Major Facilitator Superfamily (MFS) transport proteins which were discovered in Nematocida spp. (Cuomo et al., 2012) and subsequently shown to be present in all Microsporidia for which genomes are available (Cuomo et al., 2012; Dean et al., 2018; Heinz et al., 2014; Heinz et al., 2012; Nakjang et al., 2013; Watson et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Cuomo et al., 2012).

claim: The MFS transport protein family is present in all Microsporidia for which genomes are available.
source: In the present study, we have characterised a family of Microsporidia Major Facilitator Superfamily (MFS) transport proteins which were discovered in Nematocida spp. (Cuomo et al., 2012) and subsequently shown to be present in all Microsporidia for which genomes are available (Cuomo et al., 2012; Dean et al., 2018; Heinz et al., 2014; Heinz et al., 2012; Nakjang et al., 2013; Watson et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Cuomo et al., 2012; Dean et al., 2018; Heinz et al., 2014; Heinz et al., 2012; Nakjang et al., 2013; Watson et al., 2015).

claim: Some of the Nematocida proteins share a Pfam domain (PF03825) with the NupG transporter of Escherichia coli.
source: Some of the Nematocida proteins share a Pfam domain (PF03825) with the NupG transporter of Escherichia coli (Xie et al., 2004), suggesting (Cuomo et al., 2012) that, like NupG, they might be purine and pyrimidine nucleoside transporters, potentially solving the parasite pyrimidine deficit discussed above.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Xie et al., 2004).

claim: It was suggested that the Nematocida MFS proteins might be purine and pyrimidine nucleoside transporters like NupG.
source: Some of the Nematocida proteins share a Pfam domain (PF03825) with the NupG transporter of Escherichia coli (Xie et al., 2004), suggesting (Cuomo et al., 2012) that, like NupG, they might be purine and pyrimidine nucleoside transporters, potentially solving the parasite pyrimidine deficit discussed above.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Cuomo et al., 2012) and represents speculation.

claim: Trachipleistophora hominis is a model species that can be maintained in cell culture and was originally isolated from an HIV/AIDS patient.
source: To test this hypothesis and to investigate the evolution and role(s) of these MFS transporters in Microsporidia, we characterised the expression, cellular location and functional characteristics of the homologous proteins from Trachipleistophora hominis (Heinz et al., 2012; Nakjang et al., 2013; Watson et al., 2015), a model species that can be maintained in cell culture and was originally isolated from an HIV/AIDS patient (Field et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Field et al., 1996).

claim: The T. hominis MFS proteins provide no evidence that they can transport the pyrimidine nucleoside uridine.
source: Our data provide no evidence that the T. hominis proteins can transport the pyrimidine nucleoside uridine, a known substrate for NupG (Xie et al., 2004), or the pyrimidine nucleotides CTP or UTP, but demonstrate that they do transport the purine nucleotides ATP and GTP.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The T. hominis MFS proteins provide no evidence that they can transport the pyrimidine nucleotides CTP or UTP.
source: Our data provide no evidence that the T. hominis proteins can transport the pyrimidine nucleoside uridine, a known substrate for NupG (Xie et al., 2004), or the pyrimidine nucleotides CTP or UTP, but demonstrate that they do transport the purine nucleotides ATP and GTP.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The T. hominis MFS proteins transport the purine nucleotides ATP and GTP.
source: Our data provide no evidence that the T. hominis proteins can transport the pyrimidine nucleoside uridine, a known substrate for NupG (Xie et al., 2004), or the pyrimidine nucleotides CTP or UTP, but demonstrate that they do transport the purine nucleotides ATP and GTP.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Uridine is a known substrate for NupG.
source: Our data provide no evidence that the T. hominis proteins can transport the pyrimidine nucleoside uridine, a known substrate for NupG (Xie et al., 2004), or the pyrimidine nucleotides CTP or UTP, but demonstrate that they do transport the purine nucleotides ATP and GTP.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Xie et al., 2004).

claim: T. hominis, and potentially other Microsporidia, have at least two distinct transport systems for importing ATP and GTP from infected host cells.
source: These data reveal that T. hominis, and potentially other Microsporidia, have at least two distinct transport systems for importing the ATP and GTP from infected host cells, that they need to complete their intracellular lifecycles.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing both NTT and MFS transporters can import ATP and GTP.

claim: A total of 63 members of the protein family c_456 were identified among the Rozellomycota and core Microsporidia.
source: A total of 63 members of the protein family c_456 were identified among the Rozellomycota and core Microsporidia (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: Phylogenetic analysis recovered the Microsporidia transporters as a separate clade with homologues from Mitosporidum, Amphiamblys and Rozella.
source: Phylogenetic analysis including homologues from prokaryotes and eukaryotes recovered the Microsporidia transporters as a separate clade with homologues from Mitosporidum, Amphiamblys and Rozella (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2); providing evidence that the genes were present in the common ancestor of these species.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1 and supplements.

claim: The genes for the MFS transporters were present in the common ancestor of Microsporidia, Mitosporidum, Amphiamblys and Rozella.
source: Phylogenetic analysis including homologues from prokaryotes and eukaryotes recovered the Microsporidia transporters as a separate clade with homologues from Mitosporidum, Amphiamblys and Rozella (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2); providing evidence that the genes were present in the common ancestor of these species.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the phylogenetic tree topology.

claim: Homologues of the Microsporidia MFS proteins were detected in other eukaryotes including free-living fungi, Oomycetes, Metazoa, Euglenozoa, Alveolata and Stramenopiles.
source: Homologues of the Microsporidia proteins were also detected in other eukaryotes including free-living fungi, Oomycetes, Metazoa, Euglenozoa, Alveolata and Stramenopiles.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis and sequence searches.

claim: The broad distribution of the MFS genes across major lineages of eukaryote including free-living species suggests that this family of transport proteins may be ancestral among eukaryotes.
source: The broad distribution of the genes across major lineages of eukaryote including free-living species suggests that this family of transport proteins may be ancestral among eukaryotes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution of the genes.

claim: The tree topology provides no compelling support for an origin of the Microsporidia genes through LGT from prokaryotes.
source: In particular, the tree topology provides no compelling support for an origin of the Microsporidia genes through LGT from prokaryotes as previously suggested (Cuomo et al., 2012), and there is no evidence from the tree for a specific relationship to the E. coli NupG and XapB (Nakjang et al., 2013; Xie et al., 2004) transporters (Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: There is no evidence from the tree for a specific relationship between Microsporidia MFS proteins and the E. coli NupG and XapB transporters.
source: In particular, the tree topology provides no compelling support for an origin of the Microsporidia genes through LGT from prokaryotes as previously suggested (Cuomo et al., 2012), and there is no evidence from the tree for a specific relationship to the E. coli NupG and XapB (Nakjang et al., 2013; Xie et al., 2004) transporters (Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: The MFS sequences from the core Microsporidia and their close relatives clustered in two distinct clades based on the rooting inferred from a broader analysis.
source: The MFS sequences from the core Microsporidia (see Corsaro et al., 2016; Galindo et al., 2018) and their close relatives from the genus Amphiamblys, Mitosporidium, and Rozella clustered in two distinct clades based on the rooting inferred from a broader analysis (Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1 and supplements.

claim: Microsporidia genomes encode at least one member of clade A.
source: Microsporidia genomes encode at least one member of clade A (highlighted with the green box).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: All Microsporidia sequences (except one) in clade A possess a distinctive indel.
source: All Microsporidia sequences (except one - arrowhead) in clade A possess a distinctive indel (see main text and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Some sequences from the Rozellomycota including Rozella allomycis, Mitosporidium daphniae and Amphiamblys sp. cluster with Microsporidia clade A or clade B sequences.
source: Some sequences from the Rozellomycota including Rozella allomycis, Mitosporidium daphniae and Amphiamblys sp. also cluster with Microsporidia clade A or clade B sequences (the Microsporidia clade B is highlighted with the red box).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: A number of Microsporidia and Rozellomycota species appear to have lost their clade B homologues.
source: A number of Microsporidia and Rozellomycota species appear to have lost their clade B homologues.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the absence of clade B sequences in some species in the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Lineage-specific expansions can be observed for several species in clade A or B.
source: Lineage-specific expansions can be observed for several species in clade A or B.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis showing multiple paralogues in some species.

claim: Clades A and B originated from a gene duplication in the common ancestor of the core Microsporidia and some Rozellomycota.
source: Detailed phylogenetic analysis identified two clades (A and B) of Microsporidia proteins (Nakjang et al., 2013) originating from a gene duplication in the common ancestor of the core Microsporidia and some Rozellomycota (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the phylogenetic tree topology shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Clade A contains at least one copy from every Microsporidia genome sampled.
source: Clade A contains at least one copy from every Microsporidia genome sampled.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Clade B contains sequences from most Microsporidia apart from the Encephalitozoon/Nosema/Ordospora and Enterocytozoon/Vittaforma lineages, which appear to have lost the genes for these transporters.
source: Clade B contains sequences from most Microsporidia apart from the Encephalitozoon/Nosema/Ordospora and Enterocytozoon/Vittaforma lineages, which appear to have lost the genes for these transporters (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: The majority of the Microsporidia sequences from clade A contain an indel between the 7th and 8th transmembrane domains compared to other proteins.
source: The majority of the Microsporidia sequences from clade A contain an indel (insertion or deletion) between the 7th and 8th transmembrane domains (TMD) compared to other proteins (Nakjang et al., 2013) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The indel in clade A sequences is between 16 to 38 residues long.
source: The indel is between 16 to 38 residues long (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) apart from one of the paralogues from Anncaliia algerae which has lost most of the indel (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: One of the paralogues from Anncaliia algerae has lost most of the indel.
source: The indel is between 16 to 38 residues long (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) apart from one of the paralogues from Anncaliia algerae which has lost most of the indel (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The sequences from Rozella, Mitosporidium and Amphiamblys at the base of clade A do not possess the indel.
source: The sequences from Rozella, Mitosporidium and Amphiamblys at the base of clade A do not possess the indel (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: In clade A, T. hominis and some other microsporidian genomes encode only a single gene, whereas others have multiple paralogues.
source: For example, in clade A, T. hominis and some other microsporidian genomes encode only a single gene, whereas others have multiple paralogues (Figure 1, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: In clade B, T. hominis has three paralogues, whereas other species have only a single gene or appear to have lost their clade B homologue altogether.
source: In clade B, T. hominis has three paralogues, whereas other species have only a single gene or appear to have lost their clade B homologue altogether (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Lineage-specific gene duplication is a feature of the evolution of other Microsporidia transporters.
source: This type of lineage-specific gene duplication is a feature of the evolution of other Microsporidia transporters (Nakjang et al., 2013) providing the raw material (new genes) for functional divergence among paralogues (Dean et al., 2018; Heinz et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Nakjang et al., 2013).

claim: Lineage-specific gene duplication provides the raw material (new genes) for functional divergence among paralogues.
source: This type of lineage-specific gene duplication is a feature of the evolution of other Microsporidia transporters (Nakjang et al., 2013) providing the raw material (new genes) for functional divergence among paralogues (Dean et al., 2018; Heinz et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Dean et al., 2018; Heinz et al., 2014) and represents established knowledge.

claim: The Microsporidia members of clade A, one sequence from Mitosporidium daphniae and four from Rozella allomycis matched the MFS profile PF03825 found in nucleoside/H+ symporters including E. coli NupG.
source: The Microsporidia members of clade A, one sequence from Mitosporidium daphniae and four from Rozella allomycis matched the MFS profile PF03825 found in nucleoside/H+ symporters including E. coli NupG.
evidence: The claim is supported by HMMer searches against the Pfam domain database.

claim: The MFS profile PF03825 did not match any of the other transporter homologues, including the proteins from Amphiamblys sp.
source: This profile did not match any of the other transporter homologues, including the proteins from Amphiamblys sp. (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by HMMer searches against the Pfam domain database.

claim: Microsporidia sequences from clade B were characterised by matches to the more general MFS transporter profiles MFS_1 (PF07690) and MFS_2 (PF13347).
source: Microsporidia sequences from clade B were characterised by matches to the more general MFS transporter profiles MFS_1 (PF07690) and MFS_2 (PF13347) (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by HMMer searches against the Pfam domain database.

claim: The alignment for the indel in sequences from clade A did not generate a significant hit in a HHPred profile-profile search of gene families in the protein domain databases.
source: The alignment for the indel in sequences from clade A did not generate a significant hit (all e-values ≥ 13) in a HHPred profile-profile search of gene families in the protein domain databases (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by HHPred profile-profile search results.

claim: The Microsporidia MFS transporters are predicted to have 12 alpha helical TMD, with both termini facing the cytoplasmic side.
source: The Microsporidia MFS transporters are predicted to have 12 alpha helical TMD, with both termini facing the cytoplasmic side (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by topology prediction analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The predicted 12 alpha helical TMD conformation with both termini facing the cytoplasmic side is a typical conformation for MFS transporters.
source: This is a typical conformation (Reddy et al., 2012) as previously reported for the E. coli NupG and XapB nucleoside/H+ symporters (Nørholm and Dandanell, 2001; Vaziri et al., 2013; Xie et al., 2004) and is consistent with the Microsporidia proteins being functional MFS transporters.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Reddy et al., 2012; Nørholm and Dandanell, 2001; Vaziri et al., 2013; Xie et al., 2004).

claim: The predicted topology is consistent with the Microsporidia proteins being functional MFS transporters.
source: This is a typical conformation (Reddy et al., 2012) as previously reported for the E. coli NupG and XapB nucleoside/H+ symporters (Nørholm and Dandanell, 2001; Vaziri et al., 2013; Xie et al., 2004) and is consistent with the Microsporidia proteins being functional MFS transporters.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the similarity to known MFS transporters.

claim: All the Microsporidia proteins are members of the major facilitator family (MFS) of transport proteins.
source: In summary, all the Microsporidia proteins are members of the major facilitator family (MFS) of transport proteins, but there is no compelling evidence for a particularly close relationship to NupG, or strong indication from trees or bioinformatics concerning their substrates or transport mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic and bioinformatic analyses.

claim: There is no compelling evidence for a particularly close relationship between Microsporidia MFS proteins and NupG.
source: In summary, all the Microsporidia proteins are members of the major facilitator family (MFS) of transport proteins, but there is no compelling evidence for a particularly close relationship to NupG, or strong indication from trees or bioinformatics concerning their substrates or transport mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic and bioinformatic analyses.

claim: There is no strong indication from trees or bioinformatics concerning the substrates or transport mechanisms of Microsporidia MFS proteins.
source: In summary, all the Microsporidia proteins are members of the major facilitator family (MFS) of transport proteins, but there is no compelling evidence for a particularly close relationship to NupG, or strong indication from trees or bioinformatics concerning their substrates or transport mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic and bioinformatic analyses.

claim: ThMFS1 mRNA was characterised by a relatively high abundance at the first time point (3 hr) followed by a gradual decrease at 14, 22 and 40 hr.
source: ThMFS1 mRNA was characterised by a relatively high abundance at the first time point (3 hr) followed by a gradual decrease at 14, 22 and 40 hr (Figure 2A) and then a dramatic increase after 40 hr during spore formation (70 hr) and maturation (96 hr), when it was the most abundant ThMFS mRNA (peaking with a mean value of 363 TPM, Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: ThMFS1 mRNA showed a dramatic increase after 40 hr during spore formation (70 hr) and maturation (96 hr), when it was the most abundant ThMFS mRNA (peaking with a mean value of 363 TPM).
source: ThMFS1 mRNA was characterised by a relatively high abundance at the first time point (3 hr) followed by a gradual decrease at 14, 22 and 40 hr (Figure 2A) and then a dramatic increase after 40 hr during spore formation (70 hr) and maturation (96 hr), when it was the most abundant ThMFS mRNA (peaking with a mean value of 363 TPM, Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A previous RNA-Seq analysis of a sample taken at a late time point in a T. hominis infection of RK13 cells identified ThMFS1 as the most abundant transcript among the four ThMFS genes.
source: A previous RNA-Seq analysis of a sample taken at a late time point in a T. hominis infection of RK13 cells, also identified ThMFS1 as the most abundant transcript among the four ThMFS genes (Watson et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Watson et al., 2015).

claim: The expression profile of ThMFS3 mRNA peaked during the early stages of infection at the 3 hr post-infection time-point (238 TPM), and gradually declined to about 50% of this level by the 22 hr time point.
source: By contrast, the expression profile of ThMFS3 mRNA peaked during the early stages of infection at the 3 hr post-infection time-point (238 TPM), and gradually declined to about 50% of this level by the 22 hr time point (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: ThMFS2 and ThMFS4 were both characterised by significantly lower levels of transcript abundance throughout the infection, with mean levels at all time points below 19 TPM.
source: ThMFS2 and ThMFS4 were both characterised by significantly lower levels of transcript abundance throughout the infection, with mean levels at all time points below 19 TPM.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-Seq data.

claim: Published RNA-Seq data for other Microsporidia show similar patterns in the expression of paralogous MFS-like genes.
source: Published RNA-Seq data for other Microsporidia (Cuomo et al., 2012; Desjardins et al., 2015; Grisdale et al., 2013) show similar patterns in the expression of paralogous MFS-like genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Cuomo et al., 2012; Desjardins et al., 2015; Grisdale et al., 2013) and data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Vavraia culicis orthologue of ThMFS1 shows its highest expression during spore formation.
source: For example, the Vavraia culicis orthologue of ThMFS1 (Figure 1) shows its highest expression during spore formation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and the V. culicis orthologues for ThMFS2 and ThMFS4 (Figure 1) have the lowest levels of transcription (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The V. culicis orthologues for ThMFS2 and ThMFS4 have the lowest levels of transcription.
source: For example, the Vavraia culicis orthologue of ThMFS1 (Figure 1) shows its highest expression during spore formation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and the V. culicis orthologues for ThMFS2 and ThMFS4 (Figure 1) have the lowest levels of transcription (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: ThMFS2 and ThMFS4 are evolving much faster than ThMFS3 based upon the branch lengths in the phylogenetic tree.
source: Based upon the branch lengths in the phylogenetic tree (Figure 1), ThMFS2 and ThMFS4 are evolving much faster than ThMFS3 (Figure 1) and ThMFS2 and ThMFS4 also have the highest number of single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) among the ThMFS homologues (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is inferred from branch lengths in the phylogenetic tree shown in Figure 1.

claim: ThMFS2 and ThMFS4 have the highest number of single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) among the ThMFS homologues.
source: Based upon the branch lengths in the phylogenetic tree (Figure 1), ThMFS2 and ThMFS4 are evolving much faster than ThMFS3 (Figure 1) and ThMFS2 and ThMFS4 also have the highest number of single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) among the ThMFS homologues (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by SNP data in Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: Previous work on the T. hominis NTT demonstrated a similar reciprocal relationship between the degree of ThNTT sequence conservation (expressed as tree branch lengths) and expression levels, with the fastest evolving ThNTT paralogues showing the lowest expression levels.
source: Previous work (Dean et al., 2018) on the T. hominis NTT (ThNTT) demonstrated a similar reciprocal relationship between the degree of ThNTT sequence conservation (expressed as tree branch lengths) and expression levels, with the fastest evolving ThNTT paralogues showing the lowest expression levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Dean et al., 2018).

claim: ThMFS1 and ThMFS3 are characterised by higher levels of expression than ThNTT1-3 throughout the time course of the experiments.
source: Comparing ThMFS and ThNTT (Dean et al., 2018) transcript abundance indicated that ThMFS1 and ThMFS3 are characterised by higher levels of expression than ThNTT1-3 throughout the time course of the experiments (Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-Seq data in Figure 2—source data 2.

claim: ThNTT4 is characterised by the highest level of transcripts among all ThMFS and ThNTT transporters, with mean TPM values of >1000 across six different time points of the synchronised infection.
source: Notably, ThNTT4 is characterised by the highest level of transcripts among all ThMFS and ThNTT transporters, with mean TPM values of >1000 across six different time points of the synchronised infection (Figure 2—source data 2) (Dean et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-Seq data in Figure 2—source data 2 and citation (Dean et al., 2018).

claim: The antisera to ThMFS1 and ThMFS3 gave clear and specific labelling of the surface of parasites consistent with a plasma membrane location in samples taken during the time course of infection.
source: The antisera to ThMFS1 and ThMFS3 gave clear and specific labelling of the surface of parasites consistent with a plasma membrane location (Heinz et al., 2014) in samples taken during the time course of infection (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by IFA data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: No parasite specific IFA signals were detected for the antisera to ThMFS2 and ThMFS4 at any stage of the infection cycle.
source: By contrast, no parasite specific IFA signals were detected for the antisera to ThMFS2 and ThMFS4 at any stage of the infection cycle, despite observing consistent labelling of the mitosomes and nuclei of parasites (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by IFA data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The expression levels of ThMFS2 and ThMFS4 were much lower than for ThMFS1 and ThMFS3.
source: The reasons for the lack of ThMFS2 and ThMFS4 signals are not known but the expression levels of these two genes were much lower than for ThMFS1 and ThMFS3 (Figure 2A), so it is possible that the antibodies we used were insufficiently sensitive to detect expression in our model system or the proteins were not expressed under the experimental conditions used.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: It is possible that the antibodies used were insufficiently sensitive to detect ThMFS2 and ThMFS4 expression in the model system or the proteins were not expressed under the experimental conditions used.
source: The reasons for the lack of ThMFS2 and ThMFS4 signals are not known but the expression levels of these two genes were much lower than for ThMFS1 and ThMFS3 (Figure 2A), so it is possible that the antibodies we used were insufficiently sensitive to detect expression in our model system or the proteins were not expressed under the experimental conditions used.
evidence: The claim represents speculation about the reasons for lack of detection.

claim: The antisera for ThMFS2 and ThMFS4 gave no parasite-specific signal in western blot analyses on total protein extracts from T. hominis infected RK13 cells and T. hominis spores, in contrast to the strong signals for antisera to ThMFS1 and ThMFS3.
source: Consistent with these possibilities, the antisera for ThMFS2 and ThMFS4 gave no parasite-specific signal in western blot analyses on total protein extracts from T. hominis infected RK13 cells and T. hominis spores, in contrast to the strong signals for antisera to ThMFS1 and ThMFS3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: The antisera for ThMFS2 and ThMFS4 generated relatively weaker signals against the peptides used as antigens in dot blots suggesting the antibodies may be ineffective.
source: The antisera for ThMFS2 and ThMFS4 also generated relatively weaker signals against the peptides used as antigens in dot blots suggesting the antibodies may be ineffective (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by dot blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: The antisera for ThMFS1 and ThMFS3 showed different patterns of parasite labelling during the infection, suggesting that they have evolved functional differences following gene duplication.
source: The antisera for ThMFS1 and ThMFS3 showed different patterns of parasite labelling during the infection (Figure 2C), suggesting that they have evolved functional differences following gene duplication, as previously shown for the paralogous NTT transporters of T. hominis (Dean et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the different IFA patterns shown in Figure 2C and supported by citation (Dean et al., 2018).

claim: No labelling of the parasite surface by the antisera to ThMFS1 was detected in replicate slides at 3 hr post-infection, despite transcript levels for the gene being relatively high at this point.
source: We detected no labelling of the parasite surface by the antisera to ThMFS1 in replicate slides at 3 hr post-infection, despite transcript levels for the gene being relatively high at this point (Figure 2A) and clear labelling of mitosomes and nuclei on the same slides (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by IFA data shown in Figure 2C and RNA-Seq data in Figure 2A.

claim: The ThMFS1 antisera gave strong labelling of the surface of parasites at 14 hr, 22 hr and 40 hr post-infection.
source: The ThMFS1 antisera gave strong labelling of the surface of parasites at 14 hr, 22 hr and 40 hr post-infection (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by IFA data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: At 70 hr and 96 hr post-infection, strong ThMFS1 signal was located in the SPOV membrane surrounding groups of T. hominis sporonts and spores.
source: At 70 hr and 96 hr post-infection, strong signal was located in the SPOV membrane surrounding groups of T. hominis (Figure 2C) sporonts and spores (Hollister et al., 1996; Watson et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by IFA data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: ThMFS1 has a role in supporting parasite development within the SPOV.
source: This suggests that ThMFS1 has a role in supporting parasite development within the SPOV.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the localization of ThMFS1 to the SPOV membrane.

claim: The spores inside the SPOV were not labelled with either of the antibodies or by DAPI, suggesting that the developing spore coat may exclude access of these reagents.
source: The spores inside the SPOV were not labelled with either of the antibodies or by DAPI, suggesting that the developing spore coat may exclude access of these reagents.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of labeling of spores.

claim: A lack of signal from spores in these types of experiments has previously been observed using antibodies to the ThNTT transporters and to several mitosomal proteins.
source: A lack of signal from spores in these types of experiments has previously been observed using antibodies to the ThNTT transporters and to several mitosomal proteins (Dean et al., 2018; Freibert et al., 2017; Goldberg et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Dean et al., 2018; Freibert et al., 2017; Goldberg et al., 2008).

claim: Proteomics data for purified T. hominis spores has shown that ThMFS1 is present in spores.
source: Proteomics data for purified T. hominis spores (Heinz et al., 2012) has shown, however, that ThMFS1 is present in spores.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Heinz et al., 2012).

claim: Strong parasite surface labelling by antisera to ThMFS3 was detected from 3 hr up to 40 hr post-infection.
source: We detected strong parasite surface labelling by antisera to ThMFS3 from 3 hr up to 40 hr post-infection, but no labelling by antisera to ThMFS3 of either parasites or SPOV membrane in slides for 70 hr and 96 hr (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by IFA data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: No labelling by antisera to ThMFS3 of either parasites or SPOV membrane was detected in slides for 70 hr and 96 hr.
source: We detected strong parasite surface labelling by antisera to ThMFS3 from 3 hr up to 40 hr post-infection, but no labelling by antisera to ThMFS3 of either parasites or SPOV membrane in slides for 70 hr and 96 hr (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by IFA data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The absence of signal for ThMFS3 on the surface of mature vegetative cells at 70 hr appears to be stage specific because fields of highly infected RK13 cells that contain a mix of mature and early stage parasites (through reinfection), show strongly labelled smaller cells.
source: The absence of signal for ThMFS3 on the surface of mature vegetative cells at 70 hr appears to be stage specific because fields of highly infected RK13 cells that contain a mix of mature and early stage parasites (through reinfection), show strongly labelled smaller cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by IFA data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: Labelling of small cells characteristic of earlier time points, with antisera for ThMFS1 and ThMFS3 at 96 hr post-infection, are consistent with the initiation of new infections from germinating newly differentiated spores.
source: Labelling of small cells characteristic of earlier time points, with antisera for ThMFS1 and ThMFS3 at 96 hr post-infection, are also consistent with the initiation of new infections from germinating newly differentiated spores (Figure 2—figure supplement 8).
evidence: The claim is inferred from IFA data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 8.

claim: ThMFS3 was not detected in proteomics data for purified T. hominis spores.
source: Consistent with the absence in IFA of a detectable signal for ThMFS3 in the later stages of parasite development, ThMFS3 was not detected in proteomics data for purified T. hominis spores (Heinz et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Heinz et al., 2012).

claim: None of the ThMFS proteins transported [14C]-uridine above background levels for the empty vector control (ptrc99a).
source: In contrast to the positive control expressing recombinant NupG, none of the ThMFS proteins transported [14C]-uridine above background levels for the empty vector control (ptrc99a) (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Uridine is not a substrate for transport by ThMFS1-4.
source: These data suggest that uridine is not a substrate for transport by ThMFS1-4.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing no uridine transport.

claim: All four ThMFS transported ATP above background.
source: All four ThMFS transported ATP above background, whereas E. coli expressing NupG did not transport ATP (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: E. coli expressing NupG did not transport ATP.
source: All four ThMFS transported ATP above background, whereas E. coli expressing NupG did not transport ATP (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: All four ThMFS proteins can transport radiolabelled-GTP, but not radiolabelled-CTP or UTP.
source: Further experiments demonstrated that all four ThMFS proteins can also transport radiolabelled-GTP, but not radiolabelled-CTP or UTP (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Uptake of both ATP and GTP by E. coli cells expressing ThMFS transporters was time-dependent.
source: Consistent with the specific uptake of [α32P]-ATP and [α32P]-GTP, uptake of both substrates by E. coli cells expressing ThMFS transporters was time-dependent (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: ThMFS1-4 can transport purine and thus their substrate specificity overlaps with that of the previously characterised Microsporidia NTT nucleotide transporters.
source: Our data demonstrate that ThMFS1-4 can transport purine and thus their substrate specificity overlaps with that of the previously characterised Microsporidia NTT nucleotide transporters (Dean et al., 2018; Heinz et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citations (Dean et al., 2018; Heinz et al., 2014).

claim: The E. coli NupG transporter is a H+ symporter that uses a proton gradient to drive the transport of uridine and other nucleosides.
source: The E. coli NupG transporter is a H+ symporter that uses a proton gradient to drive the transport of uridine and other nucleosides (Xie et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Xie et al., 2004).

claim: Some Microsporidia NTTs have evolved into symporters capable of mediating the net import of nucleotides.
source: We have previously shown that some Microsporidia NTTs have evolved into symporters (Dean et al., 2018) capable of mediating the net import of nucleotides.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Dean et al., 2018).

claim: The addition of CCCP had no effect on nucleotide uptake by E. coli expressing ThMFS1 or ThMFS3.
source: The addition of CCCP had no effect on nucleotide uptake by E. coli expressing ThMFS1 or ThMFS3 (Figure 5), suggesting that they are not H+-symporters.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: ThMFS1 and ThMFS3 are not H+-symporters.
source: The addition of CCCP had no effect on nucleotide uptake by E. coli expressing ThMFS1 or ThMFS3 (Figure 5), suggesting that they are not H+-symporters.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of CCCP inhibition shown in Figure 5.

claim: CCCP inhibited import of nucleotides by Protochlamydia amoebophila PamNTT5, a known H+-symporter of GTP.
source: By contrast, CCCP did inhibit import of nucleotides by Protochlamydia amoebophila PamNTT5, a known H+-symporter of GTP (Haferkamp et al., 2006) (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and citation (Haferkamp et al., 2006).

claim: The nucleotide transport activity of some Microsporidia NTT (e.g. ThNTT4) were previously shown to be sensitive to CCCP treatment in the same expression system.
source: The nucleotide transport activity of some Microsporidia NTT (e.g. ThNTT4) were previously shown to be sensitive to CCCP treatment in the same expression system (Dean et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Dean et al., 2018).

claim: It takes at least 109 ATPs to make a single E. coli.
source: For example, it is suggested that it takes at least 109 ATPs (Phillips and Milo, 2009) to make a single E. coli, and the ATP requirement to make the larger cells of Microsporidia is likely to be considerably higher.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Phillips and Milo, 2009).

claim: The ATP requirement to make the larger cells of Microsporidia is likely to be considerably higher than for E. coli.
source: For example, it is suggested that it takes at least 109 ATPs (Phillips and Milo, 2009) to make a single E. coli, and the ATP requirement to make the larger cells of Microsporidia is likely to be considerably higher.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the larger size of Microsporidia cells compared to E. coli.

claim: Previous work suggests that Microsporidia can use surface-located NTT nucleotide transporters to import purine nucleotides including ATP and GTP during their intracellular growth.
source: Previous work suggests that Microsporidia can use surface-located NTT nucleotide transporters to import purine nucleotides including ATP and GTP during their intracellular growth (Dean et al., 2016; Dean et al., 2018; Tsaousis et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Dean et al., 2016; Dean et al., 2018; Tsaousis et al., 2008).

claim: Microsporidia have a second set of MFS transporters that they can potentially use to supplement their energy and nucleotide budget.
source: In the present study, we show that Microsporidia have a second set of MFS transporters that they can potentially use to supplement their energy and nucleotide budget.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing ThMFS transporters can transport ATP and GTP.

claim: The two most highly expressed ThMFS proteins (ThMFS1 and ThMFS3) are present on the surface of parasites (along with the NTTs) when they are most actively growing inside infected rabbit kidney cells.
source: Thus, all four T. hominis ThMFS transporters were able to transport ATP and GTP when expressed in E. coli (Figure 3C), and the two most highly expressed proteins (ThMFS1 and ThMFS3) are present on the surface of parasites (along with the NTTs; Dean et al., 2018) when they are most actively growing inside infected rabbit kidney cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by IFA data shown in Figure 2C and citation (Dean et al., 2018).

claim: The functional relevance of the transporters ThMFS2 and ThMFS4 is unclear as no evidence of their protein expression was detected in the model system.
source: The functional relevance of the transporters ThMFS2 and ThMFS4 is unclear as we were unable to detect any evidence of their protein expression in our model system.
evidence: The claim is based on the lack of detection of ThMFS2 and ThMFS4 proteins.

claim: The levels of shared sequence similarity between NupG and Microsporidia sequences are generally low.
source: However, as we show in the present study, the levels of shared sequence similarity between NupG and Microsporidia sequences are generally low.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic and bioinformatic analyses.

claim: Characterised members of the MFS superfamily that includes the Microsporidia sequences and NupG, transport a broad spectrum of ions and solutes using a variety of different mechanisms.
source: Moreover, characterised members of the MFS superfamily that includes the Microsporidia sequences and NupG, transport a broad spectrum of ions and solutes using a variety of different mechanisms (Yan, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Yan, 2015).

claim: The diversity of MFS transporters makes it difficult to make reliable functional inferences based upon sequence similarity.
source: This diversity makes it difficult to make reliable functional inferences based upon sequence similarity (Finn et al., 2016; Saier et al., 2016; Yan, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Finn et al., 2016; Saier et al., 2016; Yan, 2015).

claim: Substrate and mechanism vary among closely related Microsporidia NTT paralogues.
source: This is exemplified by recently published data (Dean et al., 2018) for Microsporidia NTT transporters where substrate and mechanism vary among closely related paralogues (Dean et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Dean et al., 2018).

claim: ThMFS1-4 do not transport uridine, a known pyrimidine nucleoside substrate of NupG.
source: In this study, we show that ThMFS1-4 do not transport uridine, a known pyrimidine nucleoside substrate of NupG (Xie et al., 2004), and that ThMFS1 and ThMFS3, are not inhibited by CCCP, a classic inhibitor of H+ symporters like NupG (Xie et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citation (Xie et al., 2004).

claim: ThMFS1 and ThMFS3 are not inhibited by CCCP, a classic inhibitor of H+ symporters like NupG.
source: In this study, we show that ThMFS1-4 do not transport uridine, a known pyrimidine nucleoside substrate of NupG (Xie et al., 2004), and that ThMFS1 and ThMFS3, are not inhibited by CCCP, a classic inhibitor of H+ symporters like NupG (Xie et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citation (Xie et al., 2004).

claim: T. hominis has a putative uridine kinase.
source: Moreover, although T. hominis has a putative uridine kinase (Heinz et al., 2012), most Microsporidia genomes appear to lack the kinases needed to utilise uridine and other nucleosides in their metabolism (Dean et al., 2016), even if they could import them.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Heinz et al., 2012).

claim: Most Microsporidia genomes appear to lack the kinases needed to utilise uridine and other nucleosides in their metabolism.
source: Moreover, although T. hominis has a putative uridine kinase (Heinz et al., 2012), most Microsporidia genomes appear to lack the kinases needed to utilise uridine and other nucleosides in their metabolism (Dean et al., 2016), even if they could import them.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Dean et al., 2016).

claim: A number of endoparasitic microbial eukaryotes related to Microsporidia have been identified and their genomes sequenced in recent years.
source: In recent years, a number of endoparasitic microbial eukaryotes related to Microsporidia have been identified and their genomes sequenced (Galindo et al., 2018; Haag et al., 2014; James et al., 2013; Mikhailov et al., 2017; Quandt et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Galindo et al., 2018; Haag et al., 2014; James et al., 2013; Mikhailov et al., 2017; Quandt et al., 2017).

claim: Phylogenomic analyses suggest that Rozellomycota taxa form a monophyletic sister group to the true fungi.
source: Phylogenomic analyses suggest that these taxa form a monophyletic sister group to the true fungi, for which the name Rozellomycota has been suggested (Corsaro et al., 2016), and that core Microsporidia form a distinct clade within Rozellomycota (Galindo et al., 2018; Mikhailov et al., 2017; Quandt et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Corsaro et al., 2016).

claim: Core Microsporidia form a distinct clade within Rozellomycota.
source: Phylogenomic analyses suggest that these taxa form a monophyletic sister group to the true fungi, for which the name Rozellomycota has been suggested (Corsaro et al., 2016), and that core Microsporidia form a distinct clade within Rozellomycota (Galindo et al., 2018; Mikhailov et al., 2017; Quandt et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Galindo et al., 2018; Mikhailov et al., 2017; Quandt et al., 2017).

claim: The core Microsporidia contains all the species traditionally classified as Microsporidia and which share diagnostic features of the group, including a coiled polar tube, a polaroplast, and the absence of a mitochondrial genome.
source: The core Microsporidia (the term we use here) contains all the species traditionally classified as Microsporidia and which share diagnostic features of the group, including a coiled polar tube, a polaroplast, and the absence of a mitochondrial genome (Corsaro et al., 2016; Mikhailov et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Corsaro et al., 2016; Mikhailov et al., 2017).

claim: Like the Microsporidia, many of the Rozellomycota lack genes for making nucleotides de novo and some have a limited capacity for making their own ATP.
source: Like the Microsporidia, many of the Rozellomycota lack genes for making nucleotides de novo and some have a limited capacity for making their own ATP (Dean et al., 2016; Dean et al., 2018; Galindo et al., 2018; James et al., 2013; Mikhailov et al., 2017; Quandt et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Dean et al., 2016; Dean et al., 2018; Galindo et al., 2018; James et al., 2013; Mikhailov et al., 2017; Quandt et al., 2017).

claim: Rozellomycota depend to some degree upon host energy and nucleotides for their own intracellular growth and replication.
source: This suggests that they all depend to some degree upon host energy and nucleotides for their own intracellular growth and replication.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of genes for making nucleotides and ATP.

claim: Rozella and Microsporidia possess horizontally acquired nucleotide (NTT) transport proteins that they can use to import host ATP, and in the case of Microsporidia other purine nucleotides and NAD+.
source: Recent work has shown that Rozella and Microsporidia possess horizontally acquired nucleotide (NTT) transport proteins that they can use to import host ATP, and in the case of Microsporidia other purine nucleotides and NAD+ (Dean et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Dean et al., 2018).

claim: The topology of the NTT tree suggests that NTT transporters were acquired by lateral gene transfer into the common ancestor of Rozella and Microsporidia and subsequently vertically inherited.
source: The topology of the NTT tree (Dean et al., 2018) suggests that NTT transporters were acquired by lateral gene transfer into the common ancestor of Rozella and Microsporidia and subsequently vertically inherited (Dean et al., 2018; Major et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the NTT tree topology and supported by citations (Dean et al., 2018; Major et al., 2017).

claim: Analysis of the draft genomes of Amphiamblys sp., Metchnikovella incurvata, Mitosporidium daphnia and Paramicrosporidium saccamoebae suggest that they lack NTT genes.
source: Analysis of the draft genomes of Amphiamblys sp. (Mikhailov et al., 2017), Metchnikovella incurvata (Galindo et al., 2018), Mitosporidium daphnia (Haag et al., 2014) and Paramicrosporidium saccamoebae (Quandt et al., 2017), suggest that they lack NTT genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Mikhailov et al., 2017; Galindo et al., 2018; Haag et al., 2014; Quandt et al., 2017).

claim: Based upon the topology of published trees, Amphiamblys sp., Metchnikovella incurvata, Mitosporidium daphnia and Paramicrosporidium saccamoebae have lost NTT genes during their independent evolution.
source: Based upon the topology of published trees (Dean et al., 2018; Galindo et al., 2018; James et al., 2013; Mikhailov et al., 2017; Quandt et al., 2017) which place these species as internal branches of the Rozellomycota, it appears that they have lost NTT genes during their independent evolution.
evidence: The claim is inferred from phylogenetic tree topology and supported by citations (Dean et al., 2018; Galindo et al., 2018; James et al., 2013; Mikhailov et al., 2017; Quandt et al., 2017).

claim: All Amphiamblys sp., Metchnikovella incurvata, Mitosporidium daphnia and Paramicrosporidium saccamoebae contain multiple homologues of the ThMFS transporters.
source: By contrast, all these species contain multiple homologues of the ThMFS transporters (Figure 1, Figure 1—source data 2) suggesting that these transporters provide an alternative and hitherto unrecognised way for endoparasites to exploit the host nucleotide pool.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—source data 2.

claim: ThMFS transporters provide an alternative and hitherto unrecognised way for endoparasites to exploit the host nucleotide pool.
source: By contrast, all these species contain multiple homologues of the ThMFS transporters (Figure 1, Figure 1—source data 2) suggesting that these transporters provide an alternative and hitherto unrecognised way for endoparasites to exploit the host nucleotide pool.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the presence of ThMFS homologues in species lacking NTT genes.
